title: Inside Google’s Efforts to Get Creatives Hooked on AI
content:
ByCorbin Bolies

I was about 15 minutes intoGoogle’s AI short-film screening when I realized I had nearly finished my popcorn.

Granted, the bag was small. But the rapid munching was a natural consequence of my piqued intrigue late last month as the tech giant showcased 11 AI-generated short films at Manhattan’s arthouse Metrograph theater. The directors — a mix of various ages, demographics and professional backgrounds — were the fourth cohort in Google’s “FlowSessions” program, a six-week intensive that gives a group of up-and-coming filmmakers unlimited access to the company’s Flow short-form AI video generator and several mentorship sessions to bring a short story idea to life.

It’s no secret that short-form videos have been a layman’s doorway into moviemaking in the AI era, with companies luring users with the notion of bringing their imaginations to life in ways unfathomable before the advent of generators. Google knows this as well, and the short-film exhibition seems as designed to present the films and the technology as it does to showcase the company’s eagerness for the film industry to embrace AI’s potential, moves further reflected in its DeepMindresearch partnership with A24and its work with filmmakersincluding Darren Aronofskyand Doug Liman.

That includes hiring a filmmaker-in-residence, Henry Daubrez, who has worked with each cohort to shepherd their ideas from concept to generated reality. Daubrez says the AI era means one doesn’t need a professionally creative background to tell stories, as those from other industries have found a pathway to tell stories that would’ve otherwise lain dormant in their minds.

“Life is messy,” he tells me in a video interview ahead of the latest screening. “Sometimes that was my dream career, and they get there. Sometimes they had [a dream] and it didn’t work out. Sometimes they had to keep in the family business. I think what AI is doing — and I understand the pushback about most people can say, ‘Hey, you have a camera on your phone. What prevents you from going outside and shooting?’ Depends what you want to say — the story, VFX is expensive, it’s still complicated to put things together. But I think for a lot of people, it’s gonna give them a new door.”

It’s a sentiment Google’s keen to put out there, from the cast of creators they’ve enlisted to the venue they’ve chosen. The sessions’ screening venue moved from Tribeca’s Roxy Cinema to the much bigger Metrograph in the Lower East Side, an ode to the cinephile demographic that reveres the theater. (A prior July event at Metrograph: Charli xcx’searly listening eventfor her latest album “Music, Fashion, Film.”)

But it’s one that still contrasts with the industry consternation around AI generators, which studios and creative unions have still torn into for scraping copyrighted content without creators’ consent. Such concerns remain evident in some of this cohort’s films themselves — the screening of the meditation-focused short ”One Breath at a Time,” by director Santiago Carrasquilla, featured a prominent shot of a Nintendo Game Boy logo that was promptly blurred for its online release. (Google never explicitly banned logos from the shorts, one director told me, though it was suggested they blur them.)

The short films themselves ran the gamut from the abstract to the questionable, with layers of emotion sprinkled in throughout the hourlong session. One, “Two Chairs,” dove into director Dion Lee’s existential crisis over whether to have children, with AI aiding in animated sequences. It’s a story rooted in emotion, a far cry from the wholly AI-generated, “Texas Chainsaw Massacre”-inspired horror short “Mascot,” which featured a costumed character in Times Square assaulting a man who didn’t pay for the photos he took of them. Another short, “Nothin’ Beats a Cheeseburger,” revolved around an alien arriving on Earth to indulge in the alleged “world’s best cheeseburger,” using real actors for the two leads while AI generated the alien’s likeness onto one of them.

The credits for “Mascot” featured behind-the-scenes shots of the two characters — the violent costumer and the frightened photographer — that made me question whether its director, short-form filmmaker Daniel Garcia, took a hybrid approach of real actors within AI sequences. But those shots, too, were also wholly AI, a choice Garcia says was a cheeky choice to lampoon those interested in how films are made but one that left me worried over whether it clouded reality.

“Seeing is not believing anymore,” he says. “So I just thought that, especially with AI, the behind-the-scenes is more important than the actual product. And I think now, because everyone has access to the tools, everyone can make cinematic stories easily, and what I find now is that most people are not interested in the actual film. They’re more interested in how you made it.”

Still, humanity emerged in Lee’s film, which physically featured the 35-year-old creative director in the six-minute project as she wrote letters to her future self and potential daughter. Lee tells me it was paramount she starred in the film because of its personal nature. “It would be weird if it was someone else,” she says.

Lee, a freelance art director who’s worked everywhere fromVox.comto the New York Times, says over drinks at the post-screening reception how she uses AI models to help generate assets, such as, in “Two Chairs,” a chair. But she understood people’s hesitancy toward the technology and doesn’t believe it needs to be forced upon those who aren’t already eager to embrace it.

“I think it’s good for things that you need but you can’t necessarily have access to on a day-to-day basis, and if you’re happy with that, then that’s great,” she says. “If you don’t need that or want that, then that’s totally fine too. I just feel like take what you can from it. It’s a tool. If it doesn’t work for you, then it doesn’t work for you.”

Still, Lee says she’d use AI to help produce other video projects, suggesting Google’s gambit — whether embraced by Hollywood or not – may pay off.
title_zh: 谷歌(Google)努力讓創意工作者沉迷於人工智慧(AI)的內幕
content_zh:
由科爾賓·博利斯(Corbin Bolies)報導

當我在谷歌(Google)的AI短片放映會上觀看了大約15分鐘時，我才意識到我的爆米花幾乎吃完了。

誠然，這袋爆米花不大。但快速的咀嚼是我上個月底對這場放映的好奇心的自然反應，當時這家科技巨頭在曼哈頓的藝術影院Metrograph展示了11部AI生成的短片。這些導演——年齡、背景和專業各異——是谷歌“FlowSessions”計畫的第四屆參與者，這是一個為期六週的密集課程，讓一群新興電影製作人無限制地使用公司的Flow短格式AI視頻生成器，並進行幾次導師指導，將短故事的想法變為現實。

在AI時代，短格式視頻已成為普通人進入電影製作的門戶，許多公司以將用戶的想像力變為現實的概念來吸引他們，這在生成器出現之前是難以想像的。谷歌也明白這一點，這次短片展覽的設計既是為了展示這些影片和技術，也顯示出公司希望電影產業擁抱AI潛力的熱情，這一點在其與A24的DeepMind研究合作以及與導演達倫·阿倫諾夫斯基(Darren Aronofsky)和道格·里曼(Doug Liman)的合作中得到了進一步體現。

這包括聘請駐場導演亨利·多布雷茲(Henry Daubrez)，他與每一屆參與者合作，幫助他們將想法從概念轉化為生成的現實。多布雷茲表示，AI時代意味著人們不需要專業的創意背景也能講故事，來自其他行業的人們找到了講述那些本來會在腦海中沉睡的故事的途徑。

“生活是混亂的，”他在最新放映會前的視頻訪談中告訴我。“有時那是我夢想的職業，他們達到了。有時他們有[一個夢想]，但沒有實現。有時他們不得不繼承家業。我認為AI正在做的事情——我理解大多數人可能會反對，說‘嘿，你的手機上有相機。什麼阻止你走出去拍攝呢？’這取決於你想說什麼——故事、視覺特效是昂貴的，將事物組合在一起仍然很複雜。但我認為對於很多人來說，這將為他們打開一扇新門。”

這是谷歌希望傳達的情感，從他們招募的創作者陣容到他們選擇的放映場地。放映會的場地從特賴貝卡的Roxy Cinema轉移到位於下東區的更大Metrograph，這是對熱愛電影的觀眾的致敬。（在Metrograph舉行的先前七月活動：Charli xcx最新專輯“音樂、時尚、電影”的早期聆聽活動。）

但這部電影仍然與業界對人工智慧生成器的擔憂形成對比，製片廠和創意工會仍然對其在未經創作者同意的情況下抓取版權內容進行猛烈抨擊。這些擔憂在這些短片中的某些作品中依然顯而易見——導演聖地亞哥·卡拉斯基拉(Santiago Carrasquilla)的以冥想為主題的短片《每次呼吸》(One Breath at a Time)的放映中，出現了一個顯著的任天堂Game Boy標誌，該標誌在其線上發布時被迅速模糊處理。（一位導演告訴我，谷歌從未明確禁止短片中的標誌，儘管有建議要模糊它們。）

這些短片的風格從抽象到可疑不等，並在這一小時的放映中穿插著情感的層次。其中一部《兩把椅子》(Two Chairs)深入探討了導演李迪安(Dion Lee)對於是否要孩子的存在危機，並在動畫序列中使用了人工智慧。這是一個根植於情感的故事，與完全由人工智慧生成的、受《德州電鋸殺人狂》(Texas Chainsaw Massacre)啟發的恐怖短片《吉祥物》(Mascot)形成鮮明對比，後者講述了一個在時代廣場的角色襲擊一名未支付拍照費用的男子的故事。另一部短片《沒有什麼比漢堡更好》(Nothin’ Beats a Cheeseburger)圍繞著一個外星人來到地球，享受所謂的“世界最佳漢堡”，兩位主角使用了真實演員，而外星人的形象則由人工智慧生成。

《吉祥物》的片尾字幕中出現了兩個角色的幕後花絮——暴力的角色和驚恐的攝影師——這讓我懷疑其導演、短片製作人丹尼爾·加西亞(Daniel Garcia)是否採取了在人工智慧序列中結合真實演員的混合方式。但那些鏡頭同樣完全是由人工智慧生成的，加西亞表示這是一個調侃那些對電影製作過程感興趣的人的俏皮選擇，但這讓我擔心是否模糊了現實。

“看到的已經不再是相信了，”他說。“所以我只是認為，尤其是對於人工智慧來說，幕後花絮比實際產品更重要。而我認為現在，因為每個人都可以使用這些工具，每個人都可以輕鬆製作電影故事，而我發現大多數人對實際的電影並不感興趣。他們更關心的是你是如何製作的。”

不過，李的電影中仍然展現了人性，這部六分鐘的作品中實際上出現了35歲的創意總監，她在片中寫信給未來的自己和潛在的女兒。李告訴我，她在這部電影中擔任主角至關重要，因為這部作品具有個人性。“如果是其他人就會很奇怪，”她說。

李是一位自由藝術總監，曾在Vox.com和《紐約時報》(New York Times)等多個地方工作，她在放映後的酒會上談到她如何使用人工智慧模型來幫助生成資產，例如在《兩把椅子》中生成一把椅子。但她理解人們對這項技術的猶豫，並不認為應該強迫那些尚未渴望接受它的人使用。

「我認為這對於一些你需要但日常生活中不一定能夠獲得的東西來說是好的，如果你對此感到滿意，那就太好了。」她說。「如果你不需要或不想要，那也完全沒問題。我只是覺得可以從中獲取你能夠得到的東西。這是一個工具。如果它對你沒有幫助，那就對你沒有幫助。」

不過，李(Lee)表示她會利用人工智慧(AI)來幫助製作其他視頻項目，暗示谷歌(Google)的這一策略——無論好萊塢(Hollywood)是否接受——可能會有所回報。
